item.title: Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
item.description: Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those US President Donald Trump has outlined under a deal with Moscow which has been criticised by Ukraine and some US lawmakers, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Olesya Astakhova, Vladimir Soldatkin
item.content:encoded: Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those US President Donald Trump has outlined under a deal with Moscow which has been criticised by Ukraine and some US lawmakers, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Monday. Trump announced on Friday that Russia had agreed to [USN:L1N45V0MW TEXT:"supply diesel"] to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine . "We will see how the situation develops further, but Russia has the capacity to increase diesel fuel exports," Novak, President Vladimir Putin's point man on oil, said on Rossiya-24 state TV channel. "By the end of the year, exports could reach 3.0-3.5 million metric tons per month, returning to the levels seen before the crisis," he said. Russia's diesel exports have collapsed due to Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and self-imposed overseas sales restrictions. Russia has frequently attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Before Ukraine launched a barrage of drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in 2024-2025, Russian diesel exports amounted to more than 3 million metric tons per month. Despite a self-imposed export ban, Moscow has continued to supply diesel to countries, mostly in Central Asia, under government deals. Russian diesel exports to Central Asia last month amounted to 427,000 metric tons, according to industry sources. Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a [USN:L6N4571B5 TEXT:"concern for voters"] and political parties ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. Trump's envoys [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"told Ukrainian officials"] last Friday that the Russian diesel deal was part of an effort to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war, three people familiar with the meeting told Reuters. The deal has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Putin to make concessions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has criticised the deal as a reversal of years of Western policy aimed at isolating Russia's economy. Zelenskiy said on Monday that [USN:L8N45Y0FT TEXT:"Russian strikes against at least six energy targets"] during its latest wave of deadly airstrikes across Ukraine showed Moscow had no interest in an energy ceasefire. BALANCING GLOBAL SUPPLY AND DEMAND Novak also said that under the deal with Trump, Russian diesel supplies will partially balance global supply and demand. "We are already seeing this effect, including in global diesel markets, where prices have fallen by around five to six percent," Novak said. In his comments, Novak also said that US figures putting at $250 billion the value of Russian resources sold to Europe were "significantly" understated. "The figure for the period from 2022 to the present day is $320.7 billion," Novak told Rossiya-24. "This is the volume of energy resources supplied to European Union countries." Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. That is less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels. Trump also said Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

item.title: Niners LB Dre Greenlaw suspended 1 game for headbutt vs. Seahawks
item.description: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw has been suspended without pay for a one game for his sideline headbutt of Seattle linebacker Ernest Jones IV which resulted in his ejection from the team's 32-29 win over the Seahawks on Sunday, the NFL announced on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw has been suspended without pay for a one game for his sideline headbutt of Seattle linebacker Ernest Jones IV which resulted in his ejection from the team's 32-29 win over the Seahawks on Sunday, the NFL announced on Monday. ESPN and NFL Network reported that Greenlaw intends to appeal the ruling. Greenlaw initially was assessed an unnecessary roughness penalty for hitting Sam Darnold after the Seahawks quarterback stepped out of bounds at the San Francisco 47-yard line on a scramble. As Seahawks players surrounded Greenlaw to protect Darnold, Jones and Greenlaw moved toward each other and went nose-to-nose. Greenlaw head-butted the helmetless Jones as officials intervened. Moments later, referee Land Clark announced that Greenlaw had been ejected based on a review conducted at the league's Art McNally GameDay Central office in New York. Per the league, Greenlaw's actions violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship." Greenlaw, 29, is able to appeal the suspension. Under the current suspension, he's eligible to return to the 49ers' active roster on Oct. 20, after San Francisco's game against the Washington Commanders next Monday. Greenlaw is second on the 49ers with 37 tackles this season, his first back with San Francisco after one year with the Denver Broncos. He has 535 tackles, 20 tackles for loss, four interceptions, 16 pass breakups and 4.5 sacks over 77 games (68 starts) with the 49ers (2019-24; 2026) and Broncos. --Field Level Media

item.title: Dating app Bumble in advanced talks to go private at $1 billion valuation, source says
item.description: Bumble is in advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valuing the dating app operator at roughly $1 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Milana Vinn, Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: Bumble (BMBL.O) is in advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valuing the dating app operator at roughly $1 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday. Shares of the Austin, Texas-based company closed around 50% higher on Monday at $3.80, marking their biggest-ever percentage gain in a single session. The company had a market value of roughly $389 million at Friday's close. Bumble and Ithaca, a holding company for technology businesses founded by Silicon Valley executives Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Reuters [USN:L6N42X0ZX TEXT:"exclusively reported"] earlier this year that Bumble was exploring a sale amid slowing growth in the online dating sector. Dating apps such as Bumble and its [USN:L4N4411ZC TEXT:"larger rival"] Match Group (MTCH.O) , which owns Tinder and Hinge, have [USN:L6N4420YY TEXT:"come under pressure"] as younger Gen Z subscribers grow disillusioned with endless swiping, leading to softer user engagement. "Going private looks less like a strategic masterstroke and more like an admission that Bumble's current strategy is failing," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. "A change in ownership will not magically fix these fundamental problems." Founded in 2014 by CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble pioneered the "women-first" approach to online dating. But after its $14 billion blockbuster Nasdaq debut in 2021, the company has struggled with a post-pandemic slowdown in growth. Under Wolfe Herd, who returned to the CEO role in March last year after stepping down in January 2024, Bumble has rolled out AI-powered features and new ways for users to connect as it works to reinvigorate growth. Total paying users for Bumble fell more than 11% to about 3.7 million in 2025, while annual revenue declined nearly 10% to about $966 million. In the second quarter ended June 30, total paying users decreased 16.4% to 3.2 million. "AI is not going to be the silver bullet, nor is another round of cost-cutting... Bumble desperately needs to give consumers a compelling reason to return and, more importantly, pay," Pescatore said.

item.title: Russian strike on Kyiv residential building kills two, injures at least nine, officials say
item.description: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, writing on Telegram, said two people died in the evening strike on the 25-story residence in the Darnitskyi district. Prosecutors said one body was found in a car next to the building. Zelenskiy said nine people were injured in the incident. Pictures posted on unofficial Telegram channels showed parts of an apartment building ablaze. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city in the northeast, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported serious shelling of city districts, with five people injured in the collapse of an entrance to an apartment building. He said residents could still be trapped beneath rubble. Further south in Kharkiv region, officials said one person was killed in a drone attack in the town of Lozova. Regional officials said Russian shelling killed at least three people in a village near Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's "fortress cities" in eastern Donetsk region that Russian forces have set their sights on in their slow advance westward. In the region surrounding Kyiv, one person was killed in an attack near the town of Fastiv, southwest of the capital, and one person was killed in the southeastern city of Dnipro. Russian attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, previously conducted chiefly at night, now disrupt daily life virtually around the clock.

item.title: EU looking at oil and gas windfall profit tax, as energy prices soar
item.description: The European Union is examining a bloc-wide windfall profit tax on oil and gas companies, the EU's tax chief told Reuters on Monday, as governments scramble for funds to help citizens with soaring energy bills.
item.dc:creator: Kate Abnett
item.content:encoded: The European Union is examining a bloc-wide windfall profit tax on oil and gas companies, the EU's tax chief told Reuters on Monday, as governments scramble for funds to help citizens with soaring energy bills. Oil and gas companies have reaped [USN:L4N45T0DM TEXT:"bumper profits "]this year, as energy prices have surged during the US-Israeli war with Iran, amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on Gulf neighbours. Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commissioner responsible for climate and taxation, said the Commission was setting up a working group to examine the merits and drawbacks of a levy and assess whether such a measure would be viable. "Citizens, and particularly vulnerable citizens, are confronted with dramatic increases in their energy bills. And some companies are reaping truly excessive benefits without delivering any additional service or any additional products. They're reaping the benefits from the world being in turmoil," Hoekstra said in an interview. "To many citizens and many politicians, that feels off... I think we all have sympathy for the underlying logic, regardless of where we exactly take the conversation," he said. Benchmark Brent crude futures prices climbed to multi‑year highs near $120 a barrel in late April and remain more than 70% above their level at the start of the year, [USN:L6N45K0CV TEXT:"boosting"] profits for [USN:L4N45T0DM TEXT:"oil refiners"] and [USN:L6N4410CR TEXT:"producers"]. Germany, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Poland and Austria have [USN:L6N44L0E6 TEXT:"urged the EU"] to examine a bloc-wide windfall profit tax. Hoekstra said Brussels would carefully assess the legal status of any potential measure. The EU introduced a windfall profit levy on oil, gas, coal and refining companies in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent energy prices soaring. Legal challenges are still pending after companies including ExxonMobil argued the measure was unlawful. "We're still litigating court cases from the decision in 2022 to do something similar," Hoekstra said. "So that is something that we need to take into account as well." The 2022 scheme imposed a minimum 33% levy on surplus profits, defined as profits more than 20% above a company's average earnings in previous years. It raised nearly €29 billion ($32 billion), according to a Commission report. Some EU countries have already introduced national windfall levies. [USN:L8N43W2XD TEXT:"Portugal"], for example, imposed a 33% tax on extraordinary profits earned in 2026 by oil and refining companies. ($1 = 0.8961 euros)

item.title: US panel approves PJM's registry of data centers, rejects plan to curtail power to them
item.description: US energy regulators said the country's biggest power grid -- PJM Interconnection -- can begin developing a database on Monday to track data centers, whose rapid expansion has driven up prices and threatened the reliability of the grid covering 67 million people, according to a regulatory filing.
item.dc:creator: Laila Kearney
item.content:encoded: US energy regulators said the country's biggest power grid -- PJM Interconnection -- can begin developing a database on Monday to track data centers, whose rapid expansion has driven up prices and threatened the reliability of the grid covering 67 million people, according to a regulatory filing. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, in an order filed on Friday, rejected other central parts of a plan by PJM to manage data centers by temporarily shutting off grid power to the server warehouses to avoid blackouts in times of high energy demand. The database approved by FERC could help the grid plan for the growth of data centers by revealing details about facilities like energy providers, in-service dates and power ramping-up schedules, as well as backup generation, fuel sources and location. FERC said that PJM could submit a revised curtailment plan but would need to address various issues, including why data centers would be temporarily shut off from the grid before other large energy users. PJM has been overwhelmed by an onslaught of data center electricity demand, which the grid operator forecasts to triple by 2030 to about 29 gigawatts of capacity in its Midwest and Mid-Atlantic territory. The rising demand has butted up against years of dwindling net electricity supplies in the region, contributing to a more than 1,000% increase in capacity costs in PJM since 2024 and a 6.8 gigawatt shortfall that could lead to blackouts. In an attempt to manage data center demand, PJM has put several proposals before FERC. In August, PJM proposed requiring new data center customers of 50 megawatts or greater in size pay to add new power supplies -- enough to cover the full electricity needs of the server warehouses -- or risk being shut off from the grid during times of power emergencies. FERC rejected PJM's core plan of curtailing data center grid access during peak demand, saying that it strayed outside the grid operator's authority. In its same August filing, PJM also proposed tracking those data centers, for which very few details about energy use have been provided to the grid.

item.title: Pennsylvania coroner reports measles death, toll rises to six
item.description: Pennsylvania's Franklin County coroner on Monday reported a measles-associated death in a 39-year-old woman with several health conditions, the state's sixth death linked to the disease.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Pennsylvania's Franklin County coroner on Monday reported a measles-associated death in a 39-year-old woman with several health conditions, the state's sixth death linked to the disease. In a statement posted on Facebook, the coroner said the death, investigated on Saturday, met the Pennsylvania Department of Health's definition of a measles-associated death. The woman had several underlying health conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment, the coroner's office said. It, however, did not give additional details, citing patient privacy. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it was aware of the information reported by the Franklin County coroner and was conducting a review of the reported death. It said it has confirmed five measles-associated deaths since late August. "Our team has reached out to the coroner's office and is conducting a thorough review of the reported death. We will update the public after our investigation is finished," the department said in a statement. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Pennsylvania's health department previously reported more than 1,000 cases and [USN:L4N45M1NB TEXT:"five deaths"] related to measles as the state continues to grapple with a rapidly growing outbreak. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not specifically confirmed the Pennsylvania cases but has said there were [USN:L4N45L13A TEXT:"two measles-related deaths"] nationwide. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have publicly disagreed over how measles deaths are defined. The CDC has shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count, moving away from reliance on reports by state health departments — drawing scrutiny. The agency has said it is working with a group of state epidemiologists on a standard definition for measles-related deaths. The agency has said its death count could change as additional information becomes available and reviews are completed. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease but can be prevented with the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, which is about 97% effective after two doses.

item.title: Austrian furniture retailer XXXLutz's German deal hit by EU antitrust investigation
item.description: EU antitrust investigators opened an investigation into XXXLutz's proposed acquisition of German peer Porta on Monday, saying the deal may significantly affect competition in several EU countries, which could then require the Austrian furniture retailer to offer remedies to address its concerns.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: EU antitrust investigators opened an investigation into XXXLutz's proposed acquisition of German peer Porta on Monday, saying the deal may significantly affect competition in several EU countries, which could then require the Austrian furniture retailer to offer remedies to address its concerns. Family-owned XXXLutz, whose brands include XXXLutz, Mömax, Roller, Braun, Home24 and Möbelix, and which also sells electronics and appliances, announced the deal in January 2025. The companies are two of the largest furniture retailers in Germany, the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The deal would combine more than 140 furniture stores under Porta's brands with XXXLutz's more than 1,800 stores in several EU countries. The European Commission, which is the EU's competition enforcer, said its preliminary review of the deal signalled some concerns, especially for furniture sold in discount stores. "Within these markets, the transaction may remove important competitive constraints between the companies, as they are among the few players in Germany, Czechia and Slovakia operating furniture retail store networks offering the full range of furniture," the Commission said in a statement. It said manufacturers and suppliers in Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland may also be affected by the deal due to XXXLutz's purchasing association GIGA International which gives the company significant purchasing power. The EU set a February 25 deadline for its decision. XXXLutz Germany Chief Executive Alois Kobler said the company was committed to the merger. "We have prepared thoroughly for this final stage of the process to ensure we can comprehensively address the European Commission's questions," he said in a statement. Porta Group Chief Executive Paul de Jong said the deal will benefit customers. XXXLutz found itself in antitrust regulators' crosshairs in July, when the EU opened a separate investigation into whether it had implemented the deal without first securing their approval. The company could face a hefty fine of as much as 10% of its global annual turnover if found guilty of jumping the gun.

item.title: Drugmaker Corcept seeks to bar ex-judge's views in Teva antitrust case
item.description: Drugmaker Corcept Therapeutics is seeking to exclude testimony from a retired federal appeals court judge supporting Teva Pharmaceuticals in an antitrust lawsuit, arguing her opinions could sway jurors without shedding light on the facts of the case.
item.dc:creator: Mike Scarcella
item.content:encoded: Drugmaker Corcept Therapeutics (CORT.O) is seeking to exclude testimony from a retired federal appeals court judge supporting Teva Pharmaceuticals (TEVA.TA) in an antitrust lawsuit, arguing her opinions could sway jurors without shedding light on the facts of the case. In a filing on Friday in federal court in California, Corcept said consultant and retired judge Kathleen O’Malley of the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit offered no technical expertise and that her presentation of legal opinions was inappropriate. "Judge O’Malley’s usurpation of the jury is particularly harmful given her position as a former jurist," Corcept said. "It is likely that the jury will not understand she brings no technical expertise in any factual area in the case and give her testimony undue weight, even though her opinions are ultimately just how she thinks the jury should decide." Teva, Corcept and O’Malley did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Teva sued Corcept in 2024, [USN:L2N3V203F TEXT:"claiming"] it monopolized the market for the drug Korlym to treat the hormonal disorder Cushing's syndrome. The lawsuit said Teva suffered "substantial lost revenue" from its efforts to market a generic version of Korlym, and seeks unspecified monetary damages and a court order stopping Corcept's alleged anti-competitive conduct. Korlym's active ingredient is mifepristone, the same drug used for medication abortion. Corcept has denied the allegations. O’Malley submitted a report as an expert for Teva in the case that said Corcept had filed “sham” patent infringement cases. Teva's lawsuit alleges Corcept pursued bogus lawsuits to thwart competition from Teva's generic version of Korlym. O’Malley served on the Washington, DC-based Federal Circuit from 2010 to 2022. She [USN:L2N2WJ2LK TEXT:"later"] worked at law firms Irell and Sullivan & Cromwell before opening her own consulting business that includes appearing as an expert for companies in lawsuits. Corcept contends O'Malley's expert report offered potential jurors no help understanding the claims in the lawsuit, in the way a doctor might testify about the scope of a claimed invention. “Instead, Teva has hired a former federal judge to do the jury’s job for it,” Corcept’s lawyers at Quinn Emanuel said. The case is Teva Pharmaceuticals USA Inc. v. Corcept Therapeutics Inc. et al, US District Court, Northern District of California, No. 5:24-cv-03567-NW. For Teva: Devora Allon, Kevin Neylan Jr and Michael Shipley of Kirkland & Ellis For Corcept: Robert Stone, Adam Wolfson and Steig Olson of Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan

item.title: Fed's Hammack backs restrictive policy, says better if it comes 'relatively quickly'
item.description: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Monday the US central bank should move "relatively quickly" to a restrictive monetary policy stance in order to control inflation she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms' price-setting plans.
item.dc:creator: Howard Schneider
item.content:encoded: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Monday the US central bank should move "relatively quickly" to a restrictive monetary policy stance in order to control [USN:L1N45M0L0 TEXT:"inflation"] she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms' price-setting plans. "I see inflation pressures as relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component. Energy has been making headlines this year, with prices rising for oil, retail gasoline, and diesel, but it isn't the whole story," Hammack said in remarks prepared for delivery to a National Association for Business Economics conference. Her remarks cited recent conversations in her district with firms planning to boost prices faster than their input costs are rising. "A restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2% inflation," Hammack said. "When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction" if inflation becomes more persistent or inflation expectations start to rise. She said research by her staff puts underlying inflation currently in the mid-to-high 2% range, and "my baseline forecast is that it will take some time for inflation to return to 2%, even with appropriate monetary policy." "Demand-side pressures coming from the AI buildout are raising prices on key computer, electronic, and high-tech components. This is raising costs for data centers, yes, but also for projects that use similar components in aviation, electricity production, and construction," Hammack said. Current data does not point to "an economy in which the crew are exhausted and the boat is taking on water. It reads, instead, as one that can handle a tighter hand on the tiller to finish the job on inflation," Hammack added. Investors expect the Fed to keep its policy rate in the [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"3.75%-4.00% range"] at its October 27-28 meeting. Hammack, a voting member of the central bank's policy committee, has been among the more hawkish Fed voices, and dissented in favor of raising rates at the meeting in July. Her colleagues, including Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, joined her in voting to raise rates in September. Hammack also said she felt it was important for policymakers to continue explaining their views, in particular providing their likely reaction to different economic data. Warsh has said he prefers a "quieter" Fed and is particularly opposed to forward guidance, or firm commitments to future policy decisions. Hammack said providing a "reaction function," however, was important so households and firms could understand how policymakers are processing new data and plan appropriately. "I have a responsibility to the public to explain why I make the decisions I make. Transparency has the benefit of allowing consumers, businesses, and financial markets to make better-informed decisions," she said.

item.title: Xpeng executive says EV maker will expand European production ahead of local content rules
item.description: Chinese EV maker Xpeng plans to expand its European production in order to comply with new European Union rules mandating minimum local content in electric cars, company vice president Yeqing Zheng told Reuters at the Paris car show.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chinese EV maker Xpeng (9868.HK) plans to expand its European production in order to comply with new European Union rules mandating minimum local content in electric cars, company vice president Yeqing Zheng told Reuters at the Paris car show. Magna currently produces EVs under contract for Xpeng at a factory in Austria. Zheng said the volume at that factory "is not even sufficient" for Xpeng's needs as the company expects to continue growing by "high double digits" in Europe. The executive told Reuters that the additional production would be in partnership with a local manufacturer either to build a new plant or operate an existing one. The new production line would focus on building “mid-level” vehicles and would need to have a lower cost base than the factory in Austria. Zheng said the new assembly line should start production by the time the European Union’s ‘made in Europe’ rules take effect. The Xpeng executive told Reuters that a decision on a new production line will be made within months. The Chinese EV maker is currently working on building out a local supply chain to support more production and it will be "challenging" to find a battery supplier that can meet Xpeng's charging needs and produce cells with the right energy density.

item.title: Musk has spent $276 million on midterms to help Republicans retain control of Congress
item.description: Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million in the 2026 US midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of it since July to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as Democrats' chances of retaking the US House and Senate have improved.
item.dc:creator: Dawn Kopecki
item.content:encoded: Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million in the 2026 US midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of it since July to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as Democrats' chances of retaking the US House and Senate have improved. Musk's largess, which was reported earlier by the New York Times, makes the world's richest person likely the single-biggest political donor in this year's races, according to campaign finance records. There is a lot at stake for Musk with Democrats in the US House of Representatives calling for investigations into his [USN:L1N3OW1IO TEXT:"government contracts"] as CEO of aerospace company SpaceX (SPCX.O) as well as his work running the Department of Government Efficiency under President Donald Trump . Here is a breakdown of his political spending, which was confirmed by a spokesman for his super PAC America PAC. Musk has spent $366 million so far this election cycle, which began January 1, 2025. At least $276 million so far has gone to Republican groups and his own super PAC since July. Of the $276 million in third-quarter donations: $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up to help elect Republicans to the Senate that is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota. $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up for House Republicans that is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican. $76 million went to Musk's America PAC. $10 million went to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton's run for the US Senate in Texas, where recent polls have him in a dead heat against Democrat James Talarico. $10 million went to the Republican Governors Association. $2 million went to the Republican Attorneys General Association. America PAC is helping Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races. The new giving will be publicly disclosed when many super PACs are required to disclose their third-quarter spending on Thursday. Musk has also donated more money through groups that do not disclose their donors, according to the New York Times report. Roughly $90 million spent this cycle paid for work done in the prior election or supported other issues, including an [USN:L6N3QE019 TEXT:"unsuccessful candidate"] for the Wisconsin Supreme Court and a [USN:FWN3M620A TEXT:"controversial program"] paying $1 million to registered voters who signed a petition supporting free speech and gun rights, according to an America PAC spokesman. Musk spent roughly $290 million during the last election cycle in which Trump won the presidential election race against former Vice President Kamala Harris.

item.title: Trump defends Russia diesel deal as lawmakers from both parties complain
item.description: President Donald Trump on Monday defended a diesel oil deal he made with Russia as lawmakers from both parties complained the agreement appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump on Monday defended a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel oil deal"] he made with Russia as lawmakers from both parties complained the agreement appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. Trump has said the deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports would help bring down high fuel prices. However some analysts doubted [USN:L6N45Y0PD TEXT:"the amount"] of diesel Trump has said Russia would provide over the next three months would do much to bring down prices, since it is equal to about 12 hours of global consumption of the fuel. On Friday, Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine . On Monday, Trump said the deal would help American farmers and ranchers. The price of diesel has surged more than 60% since Trump launched a war against Iran seven months ago, and high prices have jeopardized Republican chances to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. On Sunday a group of Republican and Democratic US senators called on Trump to "reverse course" on the [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"diesel supply deal"] with Russia. They said his deal may violate a 2022 law designed to support Ukraine in its bid to repel Russian invaders. "We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them by allowing the import of Russian diesel and risking erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries," said Republican Senator Jerry Moran in a social media post. Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as a leading factor for higher diesel prices. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST! President DONALD J. TRUMP," Trump said in a social media post. On Monday, Trump rejected criticism of the deal from members of his own party, in comments to reporters as he departed the White House on a trip to Ohio. "Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he said. "We can do a restriction on oil, but the rest of the world would be greatly, greatly affected if we do that." Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy bickered over the weekend about the Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Trump said Ukraine needs a new president and Zelenskiy promised to hold elections if Russia would agree to a 60-day ceasefire. Trump on Sunday declared that Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure. Whether such a deal will hold was unclear. "Well, they agreed," Trump told reporters. "They agreed because I said they agreed. ... That war has to be over with." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov [USN:R4N45F02J TEXT:"said"] contacts were proceeding about a possible energy ceasefire as announced by Trump. He declined to comment on whether the ceasefire would apply only to oil refineries. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy [USN:L8N45Y12U TEXT:"said"] Kyiv favoured a ceasefire, but both sides had to observe it. He said it was "increasingly clear" that Russia was unwilling to accept it as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday Zelenskiy told Fox News' "America's Newsroom" program on Monday that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries were not the leading cause of rising fuel prices. "Everybody understands that the prices on diesel — it doesn't depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia. Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking... the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

item.title: MIT files patent lawsuit against Amazon over cloud security technology
item.description: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has sued Amazon in Boston federal court, alleging Amazon Web Services' data security technology infringes two of its patents.
item.dc:creator: Blake Brittain
item.content:encoded: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has sued Amazon (AMZN.O) in Boston federal court, alleging Amazon Web Services' data security technology infringes two of its patents. MIT said in the lawsuit, filed on Friday, that the physical unclonable function (PUF) technology used by AWS to create unique cryptographic keys violates its patent rights An AWS spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit on Monday The lawsuit said that Amazon uses cloud-security technology supplied by software company Synopsys that infringes PUF patents covering an MIT professor's innovations Synopsys is not a defendant in the case MIT asked the court for an unspecified amount of monetary damages The university filed a similar lawsuit against Microsoft in Texas in May that is still ongoing The case is Massachusetts Institute of Technology v. Amazon Web Services Inc, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, No. 1:26-cv-14600 For MIT: Joshua Krumholz of Holland & Knight For AWS: attorney information not yet available

item.title: UK PM Burnham says Iran's IRGC likely behind RAF Fairford incident
item.description: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
item.dc:creator: Michael Holden
item.content:encoded: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The [USN:L1N45R08W TEXT:"RAF Fairford"] base in southwest England, which had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, became the focal point for a major security response after five British men were arrested nearby in the early hours of September 27 on suspected terrorism and explosive offences. US officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to [USN:L1N45S0OK TEXT:"launch a drone attack"], and last week US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran [USN:L1N45R04X TEXT:"had prompted a decision"] to withdraw the bombers from the base. "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told parliament. Iran has rejected any connection with the Fairford incident. "Tehran has had no involvement in this matter, and if the British government possesses any documents or evidence to support its claims, it should present them," [USN:S8N44X01J TEXT:"said Iran's Ambassador to Britain"], Seyed Ali Mousavi, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. FAIRFORD PLOT DETAILS SKETCHY Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on police bail "under stringent conditions", and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, [USN:L8N45U0PF TEXT:"have also been released"]. Detectives have said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed towards the involvement of a foreign state. British interior minister Shabana Mahmood told parliament a known individual, whom she did not name, who was based in Iran was believed to be behind what had happened. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm." Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France and Germany issued a statement condemning "Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners". "The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors," the statement said. The British authorities have for a number of years accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots and attempted assassinations in Britain using criminal networks and proxies, accusations Tehran has repeatedly denied. Last year Britain said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK. In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media. British foreign minister Ed Miliband said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador while the ministry announced two Iranian nationals [USN:S8N44301J TEXT:"had been sanctioned"]. The two men were Ruhollah Bazghandi, who Britain said was the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network which is accused of involvement in several plots against Iranian dissidents.

item.title: US yield surge triggers mortgage hedging, adds to bond market pressure
item.description: The sharp rise in long-term US Treasury yields has spurred mortgage-related hedging that adds selling pressure to an already strained bond market, though the impact is likely smaller than in past selloffs.
item.dc:creator: Laura Matthews, Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
item.content:encoded: The sharp rise in long-term US Treasury yields has spurred mortgage-related hedging that adds selling pressure to an already strained bond market, though the impact is likely smaller than in past selloffs. Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields have surged about 130 basis points and 30-year yields have climbed 100 basis points since late February, reflecting a war-driven oil-price spike that has kindled expectations for multiple Federal Reserve rate hikes over the next 12 months. The rise in yields has pushed 30-year mortgage rates to a [USN:L1N45U0QE TEXT:"nearly three-year high of 7.4%"], keeping many homeowners locked into existing loans rather than refinancing as they often do when rates decline. As rates rise, the expected life of mortgage-backed securities (MBS) extends, a shift that can make them more sensitive to further moves in yields. MBS investors often respond by either selling Treasury futures or by buying interest rate swaps that exchange a fixed coupon for a floating rate, a process known as "convexity hedging" that effectively reduces the duration of an asset. "The market is carrying a substantial cohort of mortgages originated over the past three years at coupons relatively close to current mortgage rates," said Mike Riddle, chief executive officer at Eris Innovations, a Chicago-based futures and options products developer. "If mortgage rates continue to climb and the possibility of further policy tightening remains, the expected duration of those loans can respond meaningfully to the next substantial move in rates," likely requiring additional hedging -- and additional selling pressure in Treasuries. MBS are pools of thousands of home loans through which investors receive cash flows from homeowners' monthly principal and interest payments. Because these cash flows are affected by refinancing behavior, their risk profile shifts as interest rates change. HEDGING ACTIVITY Evidence of that hedging activity has emerged in recent weeks across rates markets. By the first week of October, nine megablock trades had been executed in CME-listed Eris swap futures tied to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), each carrying at least $200,000 of exposure to a 1 basis-point move in interest rates, Riddle said. The trades suggested that investors were adjusting positions to reflect shifts in the yield curve. Daily volume in Eris SOFR Swap Futures hit consecutive records ahead of the Federal Reserve's September 16 policy meeting, including trades where investors repositioned for an expected rate increase. Open interest, or the number of outstanding contracts that have not been closed, climbed to a record 866,768 contracts on September 21, more than doubling the previous year's levels. The activity has drawn attention because convexity hedging has often reinforced bond market selloffs. The sharp underperformance of MBS and widening of mortgage spreads were also consistent with increased convexity hedging activity, analysts said. If MBS are performing particularly poorly relative to Treasuries at the same time that rates are moving sharply higher, that can be a sign that mortgage investors are hedging. According to a recent research note from Annaly Capital Management (NLY.N) , one of the largest mortgage real estate investment trusts, MBS underperformed Treasuries with comparable duration by 96 basis points in September, their weakest monthly performance since the banking turmoil of March 2023. MBS spreads to Treasuries also widened by about 13 basis points in September to 125 basis points, signaling that mortgages sold off more than government bonds, according to AGNC Investment Corp. OUT OF THE MONEY Still, how much these hedging flows are contributing to the broader rise in yields remains an open question. Analysts say the effect tends to fade as yields rise because more mortgages become locked in, reducing their sensitivity to changes in interest rates. "More and more of the MBS universe is significantly out of the money, which means they have no refinancing incentive and therefore no prepayment risk, which makes further selloffs less destabilizing," said Amrut Nashikkar, head of derivatives strategy at Barclays. Neil Sun, a portfolio manager at BlueBay Asset Management, said that if rates stabilize at their current levels, the biggest selling pressure may be in the rearview mirror. Beyond cyclical factors, the mortgage market itself is no longer large enough to exert the same influence on Treasury yields it once did, analysts said. James Wang, head of macro at US Bank, said the mortgage market is much smaller than the one that amplified bond market swings before the 2008 financial crisis. The mortgage portfolios of the government-sponsored housing enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have contracted significantly since the crisis. Fannie and Freddie were the biggest hedgers pre-crisis because they actively managed the duration gap, reflecting interest-rate risk, between their assets and liabilities. "At the end of the day, monetary policy expectations are the No. 1 driver of the selloff," Wang said.

item.title: Huracán Simón deja al menos un muerto e inundaciones
item.description: El huracán Simon avanzaba lentamente el lunes hacia el oeste frente a la costa del Pacífico mexicano, azotando estados del occidente del país con fuertes vientos y lluvias que ha, dejado al menos un muerto, inundaciones y cientos de personas desalojadas.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Fajardo, Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: El huracán Simon avanzaba lentamente el lunes hacia el oeste frente a la costa del Pacífico mexicano, azotando estados del occidente del país con fuertes vientos y lluvias que ha, dejado al menos un muerto, inundaciones y cientos de personas desalojadas. La directora de Protección Civil de México, Laura Velázquez, informó el lunes que una persona falleció el fin de semana en el estado Guerrero, donde se encuentra el popular destino turístico de Acapulco, debido a la tormenta, aunque no dio detalles. El Centro Nacional de Huracanes de Estados Unidos (NHC por su sigla en inglés) informó en su reporte más reciente que Simon se encontraba a unos 95 kilómetros al oeste-suroeste de Cabo Corrientes, en el estado Jalisco, con vientos máximos sostenidos de 165 kilómetros por hora (km/h) y moviéndose lentamente a 4 km/h. Simon, un huracán de categoría 2, se ha debilitado desde el sábado, cuando alcanzó la categoría 4. "Simon está perdiendo intensidad de viento poco a poco y podría estancarse esta semana", dijo Alex DaSilva, experto en huracanes de la firma privada de pronósticos meteorológicos AccuWeather. "Cuanto más lento se mueva Simon, mayor será el potencial de lluvia que traerá la tormenta, pero ahora mismo la mayor parte de esa lluvia se encuentra mar adentro y al sur del centro de la tormenta", añadió. Autoridades mexicanas advirtieron que Simon podría provocar inundaciones y deslizamientos de tierra potencialmente mortales en algunas zonas de la costa del Pacífico y en zonas montañosas cercanas. Los efectos de Simon se suman a los de la tormenta Rachel en Baja Califormia, que el fin de semana dejó una menor muerta por inundaciones, dijo el lunes la gobernadora de ese estado, Marina del Pilar Ávila, quien añadió que al menos 10 personas permanecía desaparecidas en el municipio Ensenada. El NHC dijo que se prevé que Simon retome un movimiento lento hacia el noroeste la noche del lunes para posteriormente dar un giro gradual hacia el noreste y que Simon se acerque a la costa centro-occidental de México entre el miércoles y el jueves y que se mantenga como huracán hasta mediados de semana. Estima que dejará entre cinco y 10 centímetros de lluvia en zonas costeras del suroeste y centro-oeste de México, con acumulaciones aisladas de entre 15 y 20 centímetros en partes de Jalisco y Sinaloa. Las acumulaciones aisladas podrían alcanzar 76 centímetros en partes de Michoacán, Colima y Jalisco, dijo el NHC. En la localidad costera Cihuatlán, al suroeste de Jalisco, las patrullas alertaron a los residentes sobre una posible evacuación debido a la crecida del río Marabasco. Durante la noche, el agua anegó las calles y las zonas bajas de la ciudad. En la ciudad portuaria Manzanillo, en el estado Colima, los residentes caminaban por casas y calles inundadas mientras marinos ayudaba a drenar el agua. "Todo se inundó", dijo la residente María Elena Vázquez desde el interior de su casa, con los pantalones remangados mientras el agua le llegaba hasta los tobillos. El CNH indicó que se esperaba que Simón produjera marejadas ciclónicas peligrosas y olas destructivas de gran tamaño cerca de la costa. También se pronostica que el oleaje provocado por el huracán generará condiciones de resaca y oleaje peligroso en el suroeste y centro-oeste de México durante los próximos días.

item.title: Nasdaq cae mientras petróleo se dispara a la espera de resultados empresariales, datos económicos
item.description: El Nasdaq cerró en baja el lunes, después de que el petróleo subió casi 2 dólares por barril tras los ataques contra un aeropuerto saudita, mientras los inversores esperan que los bancos den el pistoletazo de salida a la temporada de resultados del tercer trimestre y a los datos económicos de esta semana.
item.dc:creator: Ragini Mathur, Purvi Agarwal
item.content:encoded: El Nasdaq cerró en baja el lunes, después de que el petróleo subió casi 2 dólares por barril tras los ataques contra un aeropuerto saudita, mientras los inversores esperan que los bancos den el pistoletazo de salida a la temporada de resultados del tercer trimestre y a los datos económicos de esta semana. El S&P 500 cerró prácticamente sin cambios, mientras que el Dow Jones subió. El petróleo subió, ya que los ataques contra Arabia Saudita pesaron más que la perspectiva de un aumento de la oferta, a pesar de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, celebró las nuevas exportaciones rusas de diésel y el alto el fuego entre Rusia y Ucrania en materia de objetivos energéticos. La atención del mercado se centra ahora en los resultados empresariales, ya que se espera que los beneficios del S&P 500 se disparen un 30,6% en el tercer trimestre, según datos de LSEG IBES. Los principales bancos estadounidenses, entre ellos Goldman Sachs (GS.N) , Citigroup (C.N) y JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , darán el pistoletazo de salida a la temporada de resultados el martes. También se publicarán esta semana las cifras de septiembre sobre la inflación de los precios al consumo y al productor en Estados Unidos, así como los datos de ventas al por menor. Según los datos preliminares de cierre, el S&P 500 (.SPX) perdió 3,75 puntos, o un 0,05%, a 7.807,79 puntos; mientras que el Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) cedió 120,17 puntos, o un 0,44%, a 27.246,00 unidades. El Dow Jones (.DJI) subió 198,22 puntos, o un 0,38%, a 51.853,17 unidades. Con el aumento de los precios del petróleo, el sector energético (.SPNY) superó en rendimiento a los principales sectores industriales del S&P 500. El índice de servicios de comunicación del S&P 500 (.SPLRCL) también subió, impulsado por Meta (META.O) . Los sectores de tecnología (.SPLRCT) y consumo discrecional (.SPLRCD) fueron los más rezagados. La debilidad del sector tecnológico fue más pronunciada entre las acciones de chips, ya que el índice de semiconductores de Filadelfia (.SOX) perdió terreno y alcanzó su mínimo en tres semanas. Salesforce (CRM.N) subió tras una doble revisión al alza de BofA Global Research, que pasó de "rendimiento inferior al mercado" a "comprar", lo que impulsó al Dow a su máximo en casi tres semanas. En el sector de consumo discrecional, las acciones de Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) cayeron después de que Starbucks (SBUX.O) anunciara que no iba a adquirir la cadena de burritos. Microsoft (MSFT.O) subió luego de que su capitalización bursátil superara los 4 billones de dólares por primera vez en un año tras anunciar planes para un importante despliegue de sus propios chips de IA.

item.title: Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
item.description: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.
item.dc:creator: Leo Marchandon, Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food. The Paris prosecutor's office said on Monday that a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France", leading to food losses and fires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said. France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Carrefour (CARR.PA) said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5% of its stores were affected. Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks. Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street. Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted. "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X. Food retailers E.Leclerc and Auchan did not respond to requests for comment. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the "unprecedented" attack would represent losses amounting to "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day." Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said, "This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain." COLD AISLES CONTROLLED OVER INTERNET Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store's fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems". The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions". On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty's Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected. In a statement, French retail association Fédération du Commerce et de la Distribution called for "full transparency" from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed to protect consumers and return to normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running. DUTCH SECURITY ISSUE Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize (AD.AS) , which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a "security issue" on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution. A message on the retailer's smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a "cybersecurity incident". Online orders account for about 10% of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders. Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets. Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying "site temporarily down". It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

item.title: Hurricane Simon crawls along Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing floods and evacuations
item.description: Hurricane Simon crept northwest just off Mexico's Pacific coast on Monday, lashing western states with dangerous winds, heavy rain and flooding that put riverside communities on alert for possible evacuations.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Fajardo, Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon crept northwest just off Mexico's Pacific coast on Monday, lashing western states with dangerous winds, heavy rain and flooding that put riverside communities on alert for possible evacuations. The US National Hurricane Center said Simon was about 55 miles (90 km) west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco state at 8 a.m. (1400 GMT), packing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 kph), making it a Category 2 hurricane. Simon has weakened since Saturday when it was a Category 4 system. "Simon is slowly losing wind intensity and could ultimately stall this week and never make a true landfall as an organized storm," said Alex DaSilva, a hurricane expert at private forecaster AccuWeather. Simon is forecast to make landfall on Thursday in Mexico's Sinaloa state. "The slower Simon moves, the more rain potential the storm carries, but right now most of that rain is offshore and to the south of the storm's center ultimately sparing the feet of rain we thought this storm could initially bring," said DaSilva. Simon was moving northwest at just 3 mph (6 kph) and was expected to continue along that track before turning northeast and moving inland across west-central Mexico around midweek. Authorities said that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides to parts of the Pacific coast and nearby mountains. The hurricane is forecast to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) of rain across coastal areas of southwest and west-central Mexico, with isolated amounts of 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) in parts of Jalisco and Sinaloa. The National Hurricane Center said isolated storm totals could reach 30 inches (76 cm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The head of Mexico's civil protection agency, Laura Velazquez, said one person was reported to have died due to the storm in Guerrero state, home to the popular tourist destination of Acapulco. In the coastal town of Cihuatlan in southwestern Jalisco, patrols warned residents to prepare for potential evacuation as the Marabasco River rose. Floodwater inundated streets and low-lying areas of the town overnight. In the port city of Manzanillo in Colima state, residents waded through flooded homes and streets as navy personnel helped remove water. "Everything got flooded," said resident Maria Elena Vazquez from inside her home, pants rolled up as the water came up to her ankles. The National Hurricane Center said Simon was expected to produce dangerous storm surge and large destructive waves close to where it approaches the coast. Swells from the hurricane are also forecast to create life-threatening surf and rip current conditions along southwestern and west-central Mexico over the next few days. Following weeks of storms that have battered Mexico, at least 10 people are missing in the state of Baja California and one minor was killed in the coastal city of Ensenada.

item.title: Starbucks says not buying Chipotle, ends takeover speculation
item.description: Starbucks is not buying Chipotle Mexican Grill , the coffee chain said on Monday, quashing talk of a deal that could have been the largest-ever involving restaurants but was doubted by both investors and analysts.
item.dc:creator: Anuja Mistry, Neil Kanatt
item.content:encoded: Starbucks (SBUX.O) is not buying Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) , the coffee chain said on Monday, quashing talk of a deal that could have been the largest-ever involving restaurants but was doubted by both investors and analysts. "As a matter of policy, we don't comment on rumors and speculation, but we want to be clear we are not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson said. Chipotle declined to comment. The statement follows [USN:L6N45U0YK TEXT:"a report by the Financial Times on October 8"] that Starbucks had worked with advisers in recent months on a potential proposal to acquire Chipotle, citing people familiar with the matter. Starbucks did not respond to a request for comment on whether they approached advisers for a deal. Shares of the coffee chain were up 1% in early trading, while Chipotle, whose shares surged on the prospect of a takeover which would have reunited Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with the burrito chain he led for six years, fell about 4%. Starbucks also reiterated that its management was "laser focused" on "Back to Starbucks" strategy and had "strong momentum and confidence" in its long-term growth prospects. The company aims to share its fourth-quarter results and fiscal 2027 outlook later this month. Starbucks shares have gained 7.8% this year, roughly half the gain in the S&P 500 over the period. The chain has been closing [USN:L4N45G0UG TEXT:"dozens"] of underperforming stores as part of a turnaround led by Niccol, who has tried to draw back customers with shorter wait times and simpler menus. TAKEOVER SPECULATION The report of a potential deal last week prompted the investor community to speculate about a tie-up that would have brought together two of the largest US restaurant brands. Chances of a deal sent Chipotle shares up more than 7% and Starbucks down about 3%, even as several analysts questioned the strategic rationale as Starbucks was in revival mode under Niccol. "Rumors like these can prime investment bankers to start fantasizing about all sorts of tie-ups, but they're a tough sell. The tide has been shifting more toward divestitures than acquisitions," From Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management said. A potential deal would have created a restaurant giant with about $50 billion in annual sales, positioning it to better navigate uncertain demand from inflation-hit consumers, rising operating costs and the squeeze on profits. The burrito chain has a market capitalization is around $40 billion. NICCOL'S CHALLENGE "Funding a premium takeover price would likely require a mix of debt and equity, which would test leverage and could dilute existing shareholders while Starbucks is still executing its turnaround," Paren Knadjian, Partner at Transaction Advisory Services, EisnerAmper said last week. Niccol joined Starbucks in 2024 after leading Chipotle through a period of rapid growth and digital expansion. He was credited with reviving the burrito chain after its food-safety crises and expanding its digital business, helping accelerate sales growth. Chipotle, meanwhile, has grappled with softer traffic as consumers cut back spending, while higher food and labor costs hurt margins across the restaurant industry. Their shares have nearly halved in value since Niccol's departure.

item.title: Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
item.description: Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"missile strike"] on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis. Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted. The [USN:L1N45Q02Z TEXT:"Houthis"] have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran . Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, [USN:L6N45Y0C1 TEXT:"suspending operations"] at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major [USN:L6N45Y0GT TEXT:"energy conference"]. Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having [USN:L1N45Q02D TEXT:"re-entered Yemen's civil war"] to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September. With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off. Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday. Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure. The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans. UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals. "The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said. Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states. Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action.

item.title: Microsoft plans huge deployment of its own AI chips, with an eye on saving costs
item.description: Microsoft announced the next generation of its custom AI chip on Monday and said it plans to deploy potentially more than a million of them next year to back its internal AI services.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, Max Cherney
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) announced the next generation of its custom AI chip on Monday and said it plans to deploy potentially more than a million of them next year to back its internal AI services. The Maia 300, as the chip is called, is the third generation of the company's custom chips designed to handle AI data crunching such as coding and carrying out complex business tasks on a user's behalf. Its predecessor is already running Microsoft's in-house AI models, as well as models from OpenAI delivered on Microsoft's Azure cloud computing service. The new version comes amid a flurry of custom chips from both [USN:L6N45G0UZ TEXT:"cloud computing rivals"] and [USN:L6N42V15J TEXT:"AI firms such as OpenAI"] aimed at loosening the hold of Nvidia (NVDA.O) on the AI computing market. To construct the chip, Microsoft took a different technical path from Nvidia whose AI accelerators use one massive computing chip surrounded by high-bandwidth memory chips. The central computing processor in Microsoft's Maia 300 silicon is composed of "chiplets" — typically specialized chips bonded together — that use 2-nanometer technology from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (2330.TW) for key computing functions. Other chiplets included in the design use cheaper 3-nanometer tech for functions such as moving data off the processor and elsewhere inside the system. The Maia 300 processors will go into racks that contain 96 chips and use about 167 kilowatts of power, compared with the 142 kilowatts used by Nvidia's most recent GB300 AI server racks with 72 of its graphics processing units (GPUs). Microsoft said the Maia 300 chips will get about 40% more useful computing done per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," though it did not name the systems it used for a comparison. "It's basically delivering more intelligence for every watt, every dollar, and every byte of memory by optimizing across the entire system," Rani Borkar, president of Azure hardware systems and infrastructure at Microsoft, told Reuters in an interview. Microsoft said it plans to roll out "multi-gigawatt deployments" of the Maia 300 chip starting next year. Microsoft has said it [USN:L4N43V23K TEXT:"expects to spend"] more than $175 billion in capital expenditures this calendar year.

item.title: Wall Street’s AI bet is now too big to hit
item.description: The hurdle for continued AI-driven equity gains is strikingly high. And with cracks starting to appear in the seemingly impenetrable tech edifice, there are mounting signs AI risk is now far more than just a case of "bad vibes."
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: The hurdle for continued AI-driven equity gains is strikingly high. And with cracks starting to appear in the seemingly impenetrable tech edifice, there are mounting signs AI risk is now far more than just a case of "bad vibes." While the S&P 500 (.SPX) and Nasdaq (.IXIC) climbed to fresh highs last week, a string of negative headlines related to AI – from a shelved initial public offering (IPO) in Australia to reports that ChatGPT maker OpenAI's revenue is [USN:L4N45U1QQ TEXT:"falling short"] of earlier estimates – suggests markets could soon run into some serious obstacles. Earnings releases and forecasts from the big AI players in the coming weeks may ease those concerns. But the bar is high – very high. Analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to rise more than 30% year-over-year for the third quarter, with two-thirds of that coming from tech and AI, according to Tajinder Dhillon, LSEG's head of earnings and equity research. Some analysts say up to 80% of the anticipated increase in total profit growth from S&P 500 companies will come from this one area. Investors are right to be cautious. On Friday, Australia's [USN:P8N42P0IJ TEXT:"Firmus"], a data center operator backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , shelved its $5 billion IPO. It would have been the country's second-largest initial share sale ever, and the fourth largest globally this year. That was obviously a negative twist, but even positive news from AI firms may not be good enough. On Thursday, South Korea's [USN:P8N44T045 TEXT:"Samsung"] (005930.KS) , the world's largest memory chipmaker, said it expects to announce third-quarter earnings of around $80 billion, which would be a record quarterly profit for any tech company. On the same day, Taiwan's [USN:P8N3NB03R TEXT:"TSMC "] (2330.TW) , the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported record third-quarter revenue of $46.7 billion, beating forecasts and rising 50% from a year earlier. Yet shares in both companies fell. Of course, isolated share price moves and company-specific announcements aren't indicative of the trajectory of a multi-trillion-dollar industry. But they are part of a steady drip of less-than-stellar headlines. Let's not forget, it also emerged last week that [USN:L4N45U1QQ TEXT:"OpenAI's annualized revenue"] for September was around $50 billion, down $20 billion from previous indications. This all suggests the bigger AI picture could face some seriously harsh scrutiny this earnings season. THE HIGHEST BAR The sums being spent on the AI revolution, and therefore those required to make it profitable, are eye-watering. The total cost of financing the AI buildout from last year to 2032 is estimated at $10.3 trillion, or an average of 3.63% of US gross domestic product per year, according to Columbia University professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh . Assuming a conservative 10% return — below the 15-20% return on investment many analysts say AI investment is targeting — Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the annual revenue required "to recover the investment, replace depreciating capital, and compensate investors for the opportunity cost of capital" is around $3.55 trillion by 2032. That's more than 9% of GDP, roughly what Americans spend on motor vehicles, transport, household furnishings, clothes, and energy combined. When you consider that annual combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic is currently around $100 billion, total revenue would need to grow more than 80% a year through 2032 to get to the required $3.55 trillion total, Van Nieuwerburgh says. "If the economic life of IT equipment is shorter, the revenue requirement rises substantially," he said. BIGGEST MISALLOCATION EVER? AI and tech firms' profits have, so far, mostly met Wall Street’s soaring expectations. Can they continue to do so? JPMorgan Private Bank's Michael Cembalest says AI-related stocks, which he narrows down to 41 names, have accounted for 75% of S&P 500 returns, 80% of earnings growth and 90% of capital spending growth since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. That’s an extraordinarily heavy burden for so few companies. The outlooks provided by the CEOs and CFOs of these 41 firms in the coming weeks could indicate whether a market correction could be on the horizon – and just how large it could be. AI is far and away the biggest investment boom in US history. Could it also end up being the biggest misallocation of capital?
