item.title: IonQ to buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in up to $1.3 billion deal
item.description: Quantum computing company IonQ said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Quantum computing company IonQ (IONQ.N) said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business. IonQ said the acquisition would provide it with expanded channels to bring its quantum offerings to both enterprise and government customers, helping them deal with current threats and prepare for attacks from future quantum computers. Elisity, founded in 2019, has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide and has doubled its revenue and customer base year-over-year, IonQ said The deal value includes up to $150 million in earn-outs tied to Elisity's performance, it added The number of IonQ shares to be issued will be calculated at a price between $33.07 and $49.61 per share "Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted," IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi said, referring to the point when quantum computers could break widely used encryption Elisity CEO James Winebrenner will continue to lead the acquired business after the deal closes The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval IonQ completed its acquisition of [USN:L6N3YR0UH TEXT:"chipmaker"] SkyWater Technology earlier this year to bring semiconductor manufacturing in-house and boost the development of its next-generation quantum processors

item.title: US immigration authorities raid home of Democratic Trump critic Ilhan Omar
item.description: Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president ahead of the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Nolan Mccaskill, Andrew Goudsward, Doina Chiacu
item.content:encoded: US authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday on the Washington, DC, home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said. A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child. Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar, 44, is seeking a fifth two-year term in the US House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3. In announcing the raid, a Justice Department spokesperson said: "Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation." Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. 'SOMETHING'S GONNA HAPPEN' Trump administration border czar Tom Homan told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to address the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that "something's gonna happen" in the investigation into Omar's family's entry into the United States. "If we can prove that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we'll deport you," Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time. Monday's raid occurred a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump's party seeking to retain control of Congress. Omar, a prominent progressive, represents a safe Democratic district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points. 'DEEPLY DISTURBING' In a statement, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party's leadership in the chamber said the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions" about the weaponization of the federal government against Trump's enemies. Republicans have "relentlessly targeted" Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump's "mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," they added, and they vowed to "deliver full accountability" for a "rogue abuse of power." Minnesota Democrats also condemned the raid. "Americans see this for what it is," Minnesota Governor Tim Walz wrote on social media. "President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election." Few Republican lawmakers publicly commented. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote online: "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and removed from this country. NO ONE is above the law." Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect an election's outcome or benefit a candidate or party. It historically has avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election. George Washington University law professor Randall Eliason, a former US public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appears to be a break with past Justice Department practice of avoiding investigative steps likely to become public close to Election Day. But Eliason noted there is no way of enforcing the policy. "The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process," Eliason said. "It's not surprising that they wouldn't really care about violating this policy because they've shown they don't really care about politicizing the Justice Department in many other ways." A person familiar with the investigation said the Justice Department consulted with its Public Integrity Section, a unit that has historically advised and approved investigations of members of Congress, and acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter prior to the search. The Trump administration has reduced the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers and curtailed much of its authority. INVESTIGATIONS OF TRUMP CRITICS The Justice Department during Trump's second term in office has investigated and brought charges against a range of Trump's perceived political enemies. It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney General Letitia James and Trump's former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook. The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes. 'CREEPY OBSESSION' Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has [USN:L1N45U12W TEXT:"cast"] the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession." Civil rights advocates have criticized Trump's rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage." Trump in February said Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib, who also is Muslim, should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from." Both lawmakers criticized Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration's immigration crackdown and enforcement actions. Omar has said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to "hateful political rhetoric," especially from Trump. Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar [USN:L6N4591B6 TEXT:"was sentenced"] to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive views.

item.title: Dólar opera en máximos 18 meses ante escalada Oriente Medio, mercado espera dato inflación EEUU
item.description: El dólar cotizó el lunes en un máximo de 18 meses, respaldado por la demanda de activos seguros ya que una escalada del conflicto en Oriente Medio mantuvo a los inversores cautos previo a datos de inflación en Estados Unidos que se publicarán más adelante esta semana.
item.dc:creator: Laura Matthews
item.content:encoded: El dólar cotizó el lunes en un máximo de 18 meses, respaldado por la demanda de activos seguros ya que una escalada del conflicto en Oriente Medio mantuvo a los inversores cautos previo a datos de inflación en Estados Unidos que se publicarán más adelante esta semana. * El índice dólar , que mide la evolución de la moneda estadounidense frente a otras seis divisas, subía un 0,4% a 102,58 unidades, un pico desde abril de 2025. * Los precios del petróleo cotizaron con volatilidad después de que los hutíes de Yemen, respaldados por Irán, intensificaron sus ataques contra Arabia Saudita y de que dos petroleros fueron atacados durante el fin de semana. * Los futuros del crudo Brent subieron 1,93 dólares, a 106,65 dólares por barril, cerca de máximos de dos semanas, ya que los ataques eclipsaron el anuncio del domingo del presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, sobre un alto el fuego energético entre Ucrania y Rusia. * El precio de los futuros sigue estando casi un 45% por encima del nivel que tenía antes de que comenzara la guerra entre Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán. * La presidenta de la Reserva Federal de Cleveland, Beth Hammack, dijo el lunes que el banco central de Estados Unidos debería adoptar "con relativa rapidez" una postura de política monetaria restrictiva para controlar una inflación que, en su opinión, se ha generalizado y está empezando a influir en los planes de fijación de precios de las empresas. * Los datos semanales del regulador de los mercados estadounidenses muestran que los inversionistas han ido aumentando sus posiciones alcistas en el dólar, que ascendieron a unos 36.000 millones de dólares en la semana que finalizó el 7 de octubre, frente a los apenas 8.400 millones de dólares de hace tres semanas , en gran parte a costa del euro. * El reporte sobre la inflación al consumidor de Estados Unidos del miércoles, una de las últimas publicaciones económicas importantes antes de la reunión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de este mes, podría ser clave para determinar la dirección a corto plazo del dólar. * Los datos de la semana pasada mostraron que la confianza de los consumidores estadounidenses se deterioró aún más a principios de octubre, ya que el aumento del costo de la vida debido al conflicto en Oriente Medio empañó la visión que tienen los hogares de la economía. * La Fed subió las tasas el mes pasado por primera vez desde 2023 para frenar la inflación, y los mercados siguen de cerca los datos económicos para evaluar si los responsables de política monetaria podrían volver a actuar. * Los operadores descuentan una probabilidad del 78% de que la Fed mantenga las tasas sin cambios este mes, frente al 51% del mes anterior, según la herramienta FedWatch de CME. * El euro caía un 0,4% a 1,1156 dólares, cerca de un piso de 17 meses, tras registrar la semana pasada su quinta semana consecutiva de pérdidas, debido a la inquietud de los inversionistas en torno a la salud fiscal de Francia de cara a las elecciones presidenciales de 2027. * Frente al yen , el dólar subía un 0,2% a 158,57 yenes, en una sesión con escaso volumen de operaciones en Japón debido a un festivo, mientras que la libra caía un 0,2% a 1,3203 dólares.

item.title: Crudo sube tras los ataques a Arabia Saudita, lo que eclipsa el acuerdo de Trump sobre diésel
item.description: Los precios del petróleo subieron casi 2 dólares por barril el lunes, ya que los ataques contra Arabia Saudita pesaron más que la perspectiva de un aumento de la oferta, a pesar de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, celebró las nuevas exportaciones rusas de diésel y el alto el fuego entre Rusia y Ucrania en materia de objetivos energéticos.
item.dc:creator: Shadia Nasralla
item.content:encoded: Los precios del petróleo subieron casi 2 dólares por barril el lunes, ya que los ataques contra Arabia Saudita pesaron más que la perspectiva de un aumento de la oferta, a pesar de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, celebró las nuevas exportaciones rusas de diésel y el alto el fuego entre Rusia y Ucrania en materia de objetivos energéticos. *Los futuros del crudo Brent cerraron con una subida de 1,93 dólares, o un 1,8 %, hasta los 106,65 dólares por barril, su nivel más alto desde el 15 de septiembre. El crudo West Texas Intermediate (WTI) de Estados Unidos cerró en 93,74 dólares por barril, con una subida de 1,89 dólares, o un 2 %. *Los hutíes, alineados con Irán, reivindicaron la autoría de un ataque perpetrado el sábado contra el aeropuerto internacional de Riad, en el que murieron 13 personas y más de 300 resultaron heridas. El domingo se produjeron nuevos ataques, lo que intensificó un conflicto que podría obstaculizar aún más el suministro de crudo procedente de uno de los mayores productores del mundo. *"El impactante ataque con misiles de los hutíes contra el aeropuerto de Riad, en Arabia Saudita, provocará, obviamente, una escalada de las represalias contra los hutíes en Yemen", afirmó el inversor y analista Louis Navellier en una nota. "En estos momentos, las refinerías de Arabia Saudita están en funcionamiento, pero cinco de ellas se cerraron temporalmente cuando se interrumpió un oleoducto hacia el mar Rojo tras los ataques con misiles". *Este mes se han registrado más ataques contra petroleros que navegaban por el estrecho de Ormuz, lo que amenaza con frenar la recuperación de las exportaciones de crudo de Oriente Medio observada en septiembre. *Un petrolero fue alcanzado por un dron en las proximidades de Sohar, en Omán, mientras que otro sufrió daños al transitar por el estrecho de Ormuz, según informó la Agencia de Operaciones de Comercio Marítimo del Reino Unido. *"La sensación de cierta normalidad en las exportaciones desde el estrecho de Ormuz se hizo añicos la semana pasada. Los nuevos ataques de los hutíes contra Arabia Saudita se sumaron a ello y contribuyeron a la subida de los precios", afirmó Bjarne Schieldrop, analista de materias primas de SEB. *"Cada vez habrá que tomar decisiones más difíciles sobre qué defender: la infraestructura petrolera, las instalaciones militares, los palacios reales, los aeropuertos civiles u otros". *Goldman Sachs, en una nota, elevó su previsión del precio del Brent para diciembre de 85 a 90 dólares por barril, estimando una prima de riesgo de algo más de 20 dólares por barril. *Los precios del WTI, añadieron, probablemente se mantendrían bajos frente al Brent debido a los elevados costos de transporte entre Estados Unidos y Europa, y se situarían en una media de 81 dólares en diciembre de 2026 y de 73 dólares en 2027. *En el Golfo de México, las grandes empresas energéticas Shell (SHEL.L) , Chevron (CVX.N) y BP intentaban reubicar a su personal y restablecer la producción en sus plataformas después de que el huracán Isaías tocara tierra la madrugada del sábado.

item.title: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
item.description: The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Monday as oil prices jumped nearly $2 a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport, and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Monday as oil prices jumped nearly $2 a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport, and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week. The S&P 500 ended the session barely lower while the Dow advanced. Oil futures rallied after deadly [USN:L1N45X01E TEXT:"strikes on Riyadh's international airport"] over the weekend. The attacks overshadowed the prospect of increased supplies after US President [USN:L1N45X021 TEXT:"Donald Trump"] hailed fresh Russian diesel exports and talked about a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy targets. In coming days, US investors will focus on corporate earnings, with major US banks including Goldman Sachs (GS.N) , Citigroup (C.N) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) reporting early on Tuesday. Analysts were expecting S&P 500 earnings to surge 30.6% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. Also due out this week are September readings for US consumer and producer inflation as well as retail sales data. While the US Treasury market was closed on Monday for Columbus Day, stock investors have been wary of bond yields' recent advance to [USN:L8N45T173 TEXT:"24-year highs"] as elevated energy prices have stoked inflation concerns. "Looking out further in the week, we have some big economic reports," said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. He said investors were also cautious due to a lack of direction from bonds. "We're also waiting on earnings and that's significant. The four large banks reporting on Tuesday can have a big impact," he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 195.60 points, or 0.38%, to 51,850.55, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 4.30 points, or 0.06%, to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 120.27 points, or 0.44%, to 27,245.90. Trading volume was relatively light with 12.67 billion shares changing hands on US exchanges compared with the 20-day moving average of 17.62 billion. "There's a lot to be wary of," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut, pointing to upcoming data and earnings along with rising oil prices. "You're walking down a train line and you don't know, because it's dark, if a train is coming and so, you know, you're just being real careful," he said. With oil prices rising, energy (.SPNY) outperformed among the S&P 500's 11 major industry sectors with a 1.5% advance. The defensive consumer staples sector (.SPLRCS) rose more than 1% along with the S&P 500 communication services index (.SPLRCL) , which was boosted by a more than 3% gain in heavyweight Meta (META.O) . Technology (.SPLRCT) , down 0.9%, and consumer discretionary (.SPLRCD) , off 0.7%, were the biggest sector laggards. Technology's weakness was most pronounced among chip stocks with the Philadelphia semiconductor index (.SOX) finishing down 2.7% after hitting a three-week low. In consumer discretionary, Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) shares fell 3.8% after Starbucks (SBUX.O) said [USN:L4N45Y0TM TEXT:"it was not buying"] the burrito chain. Starbucks shares closed up 1.7%. Microsoft (MSFT.O) finished up 1.1% with its market capitalization climbing above $4 trillion for the first time in a year after it [USN:L6N45V11Z TEXT:"announced plans for major deployment"] of its own AI chips. Salesforce (CRM.N) shares added 2% after BofA Global Research upgraded the stock to "buy" from "underperform." Also eBay (EBAY.O) rose 2% after Morgan Stanley added the stock to its top-pick list. Meanwhile, Cleveland Federal Reserve President [USN:S0N44V02D TEXT:"Beth Hammack"] said the US central bank should move "relatively quickly" to a more restrictive monetary policy stance to fight inflation, which she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms' price-setting plans. Traders were pricing in an almost 22% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool, up from 17.7% on Friday. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 149 new highs and 272 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 1,888 stocks rose and 3,008 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.59-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 318 new lows.

item.title: Most Americans oppose betting on elections, government events, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
item.description: Most Americans oppose using prediction markets to bet on US elections and other government actions, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that suggests the booming markets may lack broad public support as policymakers debate how to regulate them.
item.dc:creator: Chris Prentice, Jason Lange
item.content:encoded: Most Americans oppose using prediction markets to bet on US elections and other government actions, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that suggests the booming markets may lack broad public support as policymakers debate how to regulate them. The [USN:L4N42Y0WQ TEXT:"rapidly growing prediction market industry"] led by Polymarket and Kalshi allows people to bet on a raft of events, including US elections, government policy moves and sports games, raising concerns among policymakers that the platforms are opening up new avenues for [USN:L6N44E0TQ TEXT:"insider trading"] and manipulation. The companies say they have [USN:L4N42H1L3 TEXT:"extensive controls"] to guard against misconduct, that their markets are often better at forecasting outcomes than traditional polls, and that they [USN:L6N44L0X4 TEXT:"offer unique ways to hedge"] a range of esoteric real-world risks. Yet a bipartisan majority of Americans is opposed to using prediction markets to bet on US elections , military actions and government policy announcements or decisions, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted September 30 through October 5. Some 69% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans said they opposed using prediction markets to bet on election results. Sixty-five percent of Americans opposed prediction market betting on US military actions and 63% opposed betting on government policy announcements or decisions, suggesting broad bipartisan discomfort with wagering on government affairs. Only 8% and 9%, respectively, supported such bets. The results shed more light on popular attitudes toward the nascent industry, which is marketing heavily on social media and TV even as it faces pushback from states and from Democratic lawmakers who argue the markets are unethical, socially corrosive and could undermine national security. "Everyone should make their own decisions about their lives," said Ronna Schmoker, 72, a Democrat from a Dallas suburb who participated in the poll. "But like anything, you have to have guardrails." A Polymarket spokesperson said Americans are bombarded with misinformation from various sources, and that prediction markets help provide unbiased, accurate information. "It’s why more than 90% of visits to Polymarket are to view markets, not to trade," the spokesperson said. "Recognition of the public value of prediction markets is growing, but they’re still brand new to most, and it’s going to take some time for the public to learn more and see the real value." NATIONAL SECURITY AND ELECTION FEARS HAVE STOKED DEBATE Some policymakers worry that prediction markets, which offer thousands of ways to wager on the US midterms, [USN:L6N41V1AT TEXT:"could undermine faith in"] the integrity of US democracy and enable government insiders to broadcast confidential information via their trades. Reuters reported [USN:L6N44E0TQ TEXT:"in August"] that more than 150 accounts on Polymarket International, the company's overseas market which bars US users, may have traded on inside military information, while Kalshi [USN:L1N41514R TEXT:"has suspended candidates"] for betting on their own races. Kalshi banned former Republican Representative George Santos, who agreed to pay $35,000 [USN:L6N43X19K TEXT:"to resolve government allegations"] of manipulative trading after he bet via Kalshi on whether he would attend the State of the Union address. Santos did not admit to the allegations and said through his attorney that he never intended to deceive anyone. Ninety-three percent of Democrats and 89% of Republicans said it was inappropriate for members of Congress or their staff to bet on political events, while 6% and 8%, respectively, said it was appropriate. Polymarket and Kalshi say they work closely with the authorities and routinely refer suspicious accounts, and have introduced various restrictions to mitigate misconduct. Kalshi says it does not allow trading on military operations and bars political candidates from wagering on their own races. The Senate in April barred senators, staff and other officers from using prediction markets, and [USN:L4N4051K3 TEXT:"several Democratic lawmakers have introduced bills"] to restrict the industry. "We see prediction markets everywhere, but don't mistake seeing millions of dollars in advertisements as a sign of growing support," said Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon. "Folks are rightfully concerned." The Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests many Americans are generally uneasy about increasingly commoditizing real-world events. Even betting on professional sports, a far more established activity, was opposed by 43% of respondents, while 29% supported it. "I just don't think it's good for a society to bet on whether things will turn out a certain way," said Michael Clark, a 48-year-old conservative who lives outside Dallas and participated in the poll. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS SUPPORTED INDUSTRY GROWTH The administration of President Donald Trump, whose son Donald Trump Jr. has business ties to Kalshi and Polymarket, is pursuing federal regulations for the industry, a move states are fighting. Legal experts expect that dispute to reach the Supreme Court. At issue is whether prediction markets facilitate trading in financial instruments or gambling, which is regulated by the states. State regulators say they are facilitating gambling and should be subject to more stringent state laws, while Trump's Commodity Futures Trading Commission has asserted jurisdiction, arguing the contracts are a type of financial product it regulates. "By that rationale, MGM (Resorts) owns dozens of financial markets," said Glenn Rishton, a 76-year-old Republican poll respondent in Gulfport, Mississippi, referring to the casino company. "It's effectively gambling." Three-quarters of Americans agreed, with only 8% saying using prediction markets to wager on the outcome of real-world events is not a form of gambling. A spokesperson for the Coalition for Prediction Markets said its research found that Republican and Democratic voters alike prefer a federal regulatory framework over a patchwork of state rules. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, surveyed 4,506 US adults and had a margin of error of about two percentage points. "Prediction markets should have the same level of regulations as gambling," said Janessa Manning, 48, a Democrat in Detroit. "Even though they pretend they aren’t gambling, they are."
